lr-01:
Number & Alphabet Series

Series questions test pattern recognition: find the rule connecting consecutive terms (add a fixed number, multiply, alternate two rules, or use letter positions) and extend it.

Start here

What Number and Alphabet Series are about

A series is a list of numbers or letters that follows a hidden rule. Your job is to find the rule from the given terms and use it to find the missing or next term.

Number series test your sense of pattern: constant gaps, constant multipliers, squares and cubes, and alternating rules. Alphabet series work the same way using letter positions (A = 1 to Z = 26).

6pattern families
26letters, A = 1 to Z = 26
5steps to find the rule
40 starget per question
At a glance

Topic map: the key ideas in one picture

The flow

The method, step by step

Follow the same order every time. Each step feeds the next, so you never have to hold the whole problem in your head.

1
Take differences

Write the difference between each pair of neighbouring terms.

2
Differences of differences

If the differences are constant it is an AP-type series; if they change, take the differences of the differences.

3
Test ratios and powers

Test ratios for a multiplying pattern, and compare terms with squares, cubes and primes.

4
Split odd and even

If nothing fits, split the terms into odd and even positions and treat them as two series.

5
Apply and verify

Apply the rule to find the missing term and check that it fits the whole series.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Where series come from

Setters build a series from a small rule: add a number, multiply, add a growing number, use squares or cubes, or alternate two rules. The hidden rule is always simple, so the aim is to try the possible families in a sensible order.

Letters as numbers

Alphabet series are number series in disguise. Converting A to Z into 1 to 26 reveals the rule, and the opposite-letter pairing (position plus opposite equals 27) helps when letters run backwards. Watch for wrap-around after Z in shifting patterns.

Wrong-number-out questions

Here one term breaks the pattern. Find the rule from the terms that agree with each other, then see which term fails. The wrong term is usually in the middle, and the terms around it give the clue.

How it is asked

6 question styles you will meet

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Take differences first

Subtract each term from the next and look at the gaps.

Why it worksMost number series are built by adding something, so the gaps expose the rule.

2Take differences of differences

If the gaps are 4, 6, 8, 10, their gaps are 2, 2, 2.

Why it worksA constant second difference means a quadratic pattern such as n(n + 1).

3Test ratios when terms grow fast

If terms roughly double or triple, divide neighbours.

Why it worksA multiplying series grows faster than an adding one, and the sizes show it.

4Compare with squares and cubes

Terms 2, 5, 10, 17 sit next to the squares 1, 4, 9, 16: each is n² + 1.

Why it worksPerfect squares and cubes are the most common hidden base in exam series.

5Split alternating series

Terms in odd and even positions may follow separate rules.

Why it worksThe setter interleaves two simple series so that one series looks hard.

6Convert letters to numbers

B, D, G, K becomes 2, 4, 7, 11 with gaps 2, 3, 4.

Why it worksOnce letters are numbers, every number-series trick applies.

7Look at the size of the jump

Small steady jumps suggest addition; doubling suggests multiplication.

Why it worksThe growth pattern of the terms narrows down the family.

8Mixed operations

In 2, 5, 11, 23 multiply by 2 and add 1 each time.

Why it worksSome series apply two operations in sequence, and the check 2×2+1 = 5, 5×2+1 = 11 confirms it.

9Products of consecutive numbers

6, 12, 20, 30 are 2×3, 3×4, 4×5, 5×6.

Why it worksFactorising each term shows consecutive-number products.

One-line method
Differences → differences of differences → ratios → squares and cubes → split odd and even → apply and check.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Growing gaps
Find the next term: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, __ with gaps 4, 6, 8, 10
1The gaps are not constant, so look at the gaps of the gaps: 2, 2, 2.
2The next gap is 12.
Next term = 30 + 12 = 42.
Example 2 · Constant ratio
Find the next term: 3, 6, 12, 24, __
1Divide neighbouring terms: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 12 ÷ 6 = 2, 24 ÷ 12 = 2.
2The ratio is constant at 2, so multiply the last term by 2.
Next term = 48.
Example 3 · Squares plus one
Find the next term: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, __
1Compare with the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25: every term is n² + 1.
2The 6th term is 6² + 1.
Next term = 37.
Example 4 · Alternating
Find the next term: 2, 5, 4, 8, 6, 11, __
1Odd positions: 2, 4, 6 (add 2). Even positions: 5, 8, 11 (add 3).
2The next term is in the 7th (odd) position, so 6 + 2.
Next term = 8.
Example 5 · Alphabet
Find the next letter: B, D, G, K, __
1Convert to positions: 2, 4, 7, 11. The gaps are 2, 3, 4, so the next gap is 5.
211 + 5 = 16, which is the 16th letter.
Next letter = P.
Example 6 · Mixed operations
Find the next term: 2, 5, 11, 23, __ using the rule × 2 + 1
1Check: 2 × 2 + 1 = 5, 5 × 2 + 1 = 11, 11 × 2 + 1 = 23.
2Next: 23 × 2 + 1.
Next term = 47.
lr-02:
Analogy & Classification

Analogy asks you to complete 'A is to B as C is to __' — first name the RELATIONSHIP between A and B in words, then find the option with the same relationship to C. Classification (odd-one-out) is the mirror skill: find what most items share, then spot the outlier.

Start here

What Analogy and Classification are about

An analogy question shows a relationship between a first pair of items and asks you to find the item that has the same relationship with a third item. Classification (odd one out) asks which item does not belong to a group.

Both test relationships. Name the relationship in words before you look at the options. Analogies can be about words, numbers or letters.

2

3

4

For numbers or letters, test a rule: square, cube, +k, or a position shift.

5

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

What an analogy really tests

An analogy tests whether you can see the exact relationship between two things and carry it to another pair. The relationship might be function, part, category, cause, degree or opposite. Naming it precisely, in a sentence, is the whole skill.

Number and letter analogies

These use arithmetic or position rules instead of meaning. For numbers test squares, cubes, multiples and sums. For letters test forward or backward shifts, reversal, or position values. Always check the rule on both elements of the first pair.

How classification works

In classification the odd one differs in a property that the others share. Look for a category (fruit versus flower), a number property (prime, square), a letter pattern, or a function. The shared property of the majority defines the group, so identify that before choosing.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Say the relationship as a sentence

'A Doctor works in a Hospital, so a Teacher works in a __.'

Why it worksA sentence turns a vague feeling into a rule that can be applied to the next pair.

2Keep the order of the pair

Pen : Write is tool : action, so Knife : Cut, not Cut : Knife.

Why it worksReversing the order reverses the relationship and leads to the trap option.

3Be specific, not vague

'Used in a kitchen' is vague; 'tool used for cutting' is exact.

Why it worksThe correct option fits only the exact relationship, while trap options fit a vague one.

4For numbers test squares, cubes and multiples first

4 : 16 is n²; 3 : 27 is n³.

Why it worksExam setters rely on a small family of simple operations.

5Classification: find the shared property of the majority

Four are flowers and one is a fruit, so the fruit is the outlier.

Why it worksThe odd one is defined by what the rest have in common, so find that first.

6Check letters by position numbers

CAT to DBU is +1 on every letter.

Why it worksNumbers make the shift visible and countable.

7Eliminate options from the stem's own class

If A and B are from the same class, options from that class are usually traps.

Why it worksThe right option lies in the relation, not in the class.

8Check both directions

Verify A to B and C to D with the same sentence.

Why it worksA relationship that fails on one pair is not the rule.

9Number analogy pairs

6 : 36 and 7 : 49 are squares; 6 : 18 and 7 : 21 are triples.

Why it worksTest squares first, then multiples.

One-line method
Say the relationship → apply it to the third item → reject reversed options → for numbers and letters test a rule.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Word analogy
Complete: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : __
1Say the relationship: a Doctor works in a Hospital (person : workplace).
2Apply it: a Teacher works in a ___.
Answer = School.
Example 2 · Number analogy
Complete: 4 : 16 :: 5 : __
1Name the numeric rule: 16 = 4², the second number is the square of the first.
2Apply the same rule to 5.
Answer = 5² = 25.
Example 3 · Letter analogy
Complete: CAT : DBU :: DOG : __
1Compare the letters: C to D, A to B, T to U; each is +1.
2Apply +1 to D, O, G to get E, P, H.
Answer = EPH.
Example 4 · Odd word out
Find the odd one out: Rose, Lotus, Jasmine, Mango, Lily (the shared property is being a flower)
1Four of the five are flowers.
2Mango is a fruit.
Odd one out = Mango.
Example 5 · Odd number out
Find the odd number: 9, 16, 25, 30, 49
19 = 3², 16 = 4², 25 = 5² and 49 = 7² are perfect squares.
230 is not a perfect square.
Odd one out = 30.
Example 6 · Odd letter group
Find the odd one out: CF, GJ, KN, PS, TV
1Positions: C(3) to F(6), G(7) to J(10), K(11) to N(14), P(16) to S(19), T(20) to V(22).
2The first four pairs differ by 3; TV differs by 2.
Odd one out = TV.
lr-03:
Coding-Decoding

Coding-decoding hides a substitution rule (shift letters, reverse word, code by position) inside a given example — your job is to find the rule from the example, then apply it to the new word.

Start here

What Coding-Decoding is about

Coding-Decoding hides a rule that turns a word or number into a code. You are given an example, you must find the rule from it, and then you must apply the same rule to a new word.

The rule is usually one of a few types: shifting letters forward or backward, using the opposite letter, replacing letters with numbers, reversing the word, or matching words to codes in a sentence.

1

Write the given word and its code one above the other, letter by letter.

2
Find the change

Compare each pair of letters or numbers to find the change: shift, opposite, or position.

3
Test every letter

Check that the same rule explains EVERY letter, not only the first.

4
Apply to the new word

Apply the rule to the new word, letter by letter.

5
Sentence codes

For sentence codes, match repeated words with repeated codes across the sentences.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

The three main rule families

Most codes are a shift (each letter moves a fixed or changing number of places), a substitution (letters replaced by symbols or other letters), or a transformation (reverse the word, swap letters, convert to numbers). Identifying the family from the example is half the work.

Why the opposite-letter code is easy

The reversed alphabet pairs A with Z, B with Y and so on. Because the positions add up to 27, the opposite of the letter at position p is the letter at 27 − p. Memorise the middle pair M and N and count outwards.

Decoding in reverse

If a question gives the code and asks for the word, apply the inverse rule: subtract instead of add, or read the reversed alphabet again. Test your answer by encoding it and checking that it matches the given code.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Compare letter by letter, not word by word

Write both words in two rows and compare each pair.

Why it worksA rule can differ at each position (such as +1, +2, +3), and only a letter-by-letter view shows it.

2Check the rule on every letter

If the rule works for the first letter only, it is wrong.

Why it worksA true rule explains all letters; a false one fails somewhere.

3Use numbers for hard shifts

Convert letters to positions, find the change, convert back.

Why it worksNumbers are easier to add and compare than letters.

4Opposite letters: the pair sum is 27

C (3) and X (24) add to 27.

Why it worksThe reversed alphabet maps position p to 27 − p.

5Sentence codes: find the word that repeats

The word common to two sentences matches the code common to them.

Why it worksA word has one code, so a repeated word must have a repeated code.

6Write the rule before applying it

Say 'each letter +2' and then apply it.

Why it worksStating the rule prevents applying the example to the wrong letters.

7Shifts that grow

CAT becomes DCW: shifts of +1, +2, +3.

Why it worksShifts can increase by one at each position.

8Vowel and consonant rules

Some codes change only the vowels or only the consonants.

Why it worksCompare which letters stay fixed to see which are changed.

9Palindromes

LEVEL stays LEVEL when reversed.

Why it worksA palindrome reads the same backwards, so reversal leaves it unchanged.

One-line method
Align letter by letter → find the change → test it on every letter → state the rule → apply it.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Letter shift
If CAT is coded DBU, code DOG
1Compare each pair: C to D, A to B, T to U; each is +1.
2Apply +1 to D, O, G to get E, P, H.
DOG = EPH.
Example 2 · Opposite letters
Code CAT using the opposite-letter rule
1Each position p becomes 27 − p: C (3) to 24, A (1) to 26, T (20) to 7.
224 = X, 26 = Z and 7 = G.
CAT = XZG.
Example 3 · Number coding
If DOG (4, 15, 7) is coded 8, 30, 14, code CAT
1Spot the rule: 4 to 8, 15 to 30, 7 to 14; every value is doubled.
2CAT is (3, 1, 20), doubled.
CAT = 6, 2, 40.
Example 4 · Sentence coding
'pen is good' = 'du fi ra' and 'good day' = 'ra mo'. Find the code for good
1The word common to both sentences is 'good'.
2The code common to both is 'ra'.
'good' = 'ra'.
Example 5 · Mixed rule
Rule: reverse the word and then shift +1. Code TEAM
1Reverse TEAM to get MAET.
2Shift each letter by +1: M to N, A to B, E to F, T to U.
TEAM = NBFU.
Example 6 · Growing shift
If CAT is coded DCW (shifts +1, +2, +3), code DOG
1The shifts are +1, +2, +3 on the three letters in turn.
2D + 1 = E, O + 2 = Q, G + 3 = J.
DOG = EQJ.
lr-04:
Blood Relations & Direction Sense

Blood relations become trivial once you draw a family tree with arrows as you read the statement; direction-sense questions become trivial once you sketch a simple compass diagram and track each turn.

Start here

What blood relations questions are

A blood relation is a family connection that comes from birth (parents, children, brothers, sisters, grandparents, uncles, aunts, cousins) or from marriage (husband, wife, in-laws). In the exam you are never asked to know a real family. You are given a short statement such as "A is the son of B, and B is the sister of C" and you must work out how two named people are related.

Nothing needs to be memorised from outside the syllabus. The whole chapter is three skills: (1) know the relation words, (2) read each statement for gender and generation, and (3) draw a small tree so that nothing is held in your head.

Gender and generation: the two facts hidden in every word

Every relation word carries two facts: the gender of the person and the generation they belong to. If you extract both from each word, most answers become automatic.

How it is asked

The six question styles you will meet

All questions in this chapter come from one of these six styles. The sample phrasing is the typical form. Learn to name the style in the first five seconds, because each style has its own method.

Direct chain
A is the father of B. B is the sister of C. How is A related to C
One-line or two-line statements joined in a chain. You are asked how the first person is related to the last.
Pointing / photograph
Pointing to a man, a woman said, "He is the son of my mother's only son"
The speaker describes someone with a chain of relations. First work out who the speaker is, then follow the chain.
Coded relations
P + Q means P is the mother of Q; P − Q means P is the brother of Q
Symbols stand for relations. Replace each symbol with its meaning and then solve it like a direct chain.
Family-tree puzzle
Six members A to F; clues give marriages, children and genders
Longer puzzle with several clues; the tree must be drawn and every clue ticked off. Then 2 or 3 questions follow.
Mixed-gender / unknown
Who is the maternal uncle of Z
Questions that test whether you can say 'cannot be determined' when the gender or the side is not given.
Counting
How many brothers does P have; how many females are in the family
You are given relations and asked to count men, women or a particular relation.
The tricks

Nine tricks, and how to understand why each one works

A trick you only memorise will fail under pressure. Each trick below has a short reason attached, so you can rebuild it yourself if you forget it.

1Draw, never imagine

Use + (or a square) for male, − (or a circle) for female, = between a married couple, a vertical line downward for children and a horizontal line for brothers and sisters. Put the older generation higher up.

Why it worksA tree turns a sentence into a picture, and the eye can see a relation that the mind has to calculate. Every top scorer in this chapter draws, even for two-line questions.

2Always start from the END of the chain and shorten step by step

For 'A's father's brother's son', solve left to right in pairs: father's brother = uncle; uncle's son = cousin. The answer is 'A's cousin'. Never try to jump to the answer in one go.

Why it worksEach pair collapses into one relation word, so a long chain shrinks by one word every step and you can check each step against the table.

3Use the 'only' word as a key

'My father's only son' is me (if I am male) or my brother (if I am female). 'My mother's only daughter' is me (if I am female) or my sister (if I am male). Without 'only' you cannot say it is the same person.

Why it works'Only' means there is exactly one such child, so if the speaker fits, the speaker is that child. The question setter uses this to hide the speaker inside the chain.

4Identify the speaker first in pointing questions

In 'Pointing to a girl, Neha said "She is the daughter of my father's only son"', start with Neha: she is female, so her father's only son is her brother. The girl is her brother's daughter, which is Neha's niece.

Why it worksEverything after the word 'my' is measured from the speaker. If you start from the pointed person you will reverse the answer, which is the most common mistake.

5The two-step rule for in-laws

An in-law is always my spouse's relative or my relative's spouse. 'Wife's brother' and 'sister's husband' are both brothers-in-law; 'brother's wife' and 'husband's sister' are both sisters-in-law.

Why it worksMarriage joins two families. People who enter your family by marriage, or whose family you enter by marriage, are in-laws; blood relatives of those two families are not your blood relatives.

6Generation arithmetic

Write +1 for each step up (parent) and −1 for each step down (child). The final number tells the level of the answer: +1 is an uncle, aunt or parent; 0 is a sibling or cousin; −1 is a child, nephew or niece.

Why it worksYou can instantly reject any option on the wrong level without finishing the chain. This saves 15 to 20 seconds.

7Side-pairing for uncles, aunts and cousins

Father's side: chacha / tau (uncle), bua (aunt). Mother's side: mama (uncle), mausi (aunt). Cousins always come from these four people.

Why it worksParents' siblings are one generation above you, so their children are on your own level. That is why the answer is 'cousin' and not 'nephew'.

8Coded relations: translate, then draw

Write each symbol's meaning above it, solve the first pair, then bring in the next symbol. Never solve the whole code in one go.

Why it worksA code is only a short direct chain in disguise. Replacing symbols with words puts you back on familiar ground.

9Say 'cannot be determined' only when gender or side is truly missing

If one needed gender is not given anywhere, a neutral word is the safe answer. If every gender is given, the answer is exact.

Why it worksThe exam rewards the safest correct word. A gender-specific option is right only if the statement fixes that gender.

One-line method for any question
Extract gender and generation from each word → draw the tree with +, −, =, | → shorten the chain two words at a time → check the answer against the options.
Solved examples

Six solved examples, from easy to tricky

Each example is solved on the same notebook layout as the rest of the notes. The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Direct chain
A is the father of B. B is the sister of C. D is the mother of C. How is A related to D
1B and C are sister and brother (or sisters), so they have the same parents. A is B's father, so A is also C's father.
2D is C's mother. A and D are therefore the two parents of C.
A is the husband of D.
Example 2 · Pointing question
Pointing to a girl, Neha says, "She is the daughter of my father's only son"
1Start with the speaker. Neha is female, so 'my father's only son' cannot be Neha. It is her brother.
2The girl is the daughter of Neha's brother, so she is Neha's brother's daughter.
The girl is Neha's niece.
Example 3 · Maternal side
Rahul says, "My mother's brother's only daughter is Priya."
1Mother's brother is Rahul's maternal uncle (mama). He is on the parents' level.
2His daughter is one generation below him, so she is on Rahul's own level: a cousin. Priya is female.
Priya is Rahul's maternal cousin sister. In the options look for 'cousin'.
Example 4 · Coded relations
P + Q means P is the mother of Q. P − Q means P is the brother of Q. Find A − B + C
1Take the first pair: A − B means A is the brother of B, so A is male and on B's level.
2Take the second pair: B + C means B is the mother of C. A is B's brother, so A is C's maternal uncle.
A is the maternal uncle of C.
Example 5 · Family-tree puzzle
A and B are a married couple, A being male. C is the son of B. D is the sister of C. E is the husband of D. F is the child of E and D. How is F related to B
1B is C's mother. D is C's sister, so D is also B's daughter. A is the father of C and D.
2E is D's husband, so B's son-in-law. F is the child of D, so F is B's grandchild.
F is B's grandchild (gender not given, so use the neutral word).
Example 6 · 'Only' trap
Looking at a man, a woman says, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother."
1The woman's mother's only daughter is the woman herself. So his mother is the woman.
2He is the woman's son. Many students wrongly say 'brother' or 'nephew' because they stop at the sister step.
The man is the woman's son.

Seating Arrangement & Puzzles

Seating puzzles are solved by converting every clue into a mark on a diagram (a row of boxes, or a circle) one at a time — never try to hold multiple constraints in your head simultaneously.

Start here

What Seating Arrangement and Puzzles are about

Seating Arrangement questions give you a group of people and a set of clues about who sits where. Your job is to place everyone correctly and then answer questions about positions, neighbours and directions.

Arrangements are linear (a row), circular (a table) or sometimes two rows facing each other. Solving is mostly a matter of drawing a diagram and placing the most definite clue first.

At a glance

Topic map: the key ideas in one picture

The flow

The method, step by step

Follow the same order every time. Each step feeds the next, so you never have to hold the whole problem in your head.

1
Identify the layout

Read all the clues once and identify the arrangement: a row, a circle or two rows.

2
Draw the seats

Draw empty seats (a row of boxes or a circle) and mark North or another fixed reference.

3
Fix the sure clue

Place the most definite clue first: an end seat, a fixed position, or a pair that must sit together.

4
Add relative clues

Add the relative clues one by one, trying both options when a clue is not fixed.

5
Check every clue

Check every clue against the final diagram before answering.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Types and what they imply

In a straight row, people have a left end and a right end and every interior person has two neighbours. In a circle, everyone has two neighbours and there are no ends, but there is an opposite. Two-row arrangements add an 'opposite' across the rows. The layout tells you which clue words (end, opposite, adjacent) can appear.

Left and right depend on facing

Left and right are always from the person's own view. When people face the centre of a circle, their left is the opposite of what an outside observer sees. In rows with people facing North or South, left and right swap between the two groups. Mark each person's facing first.

Using elimination

If a clue gives two possible places, draw both branches and let the next clue eliminate one. In a fully determined puzzle exactly one branch survives. Keep the other clues unused until needed, and check all clues at the end.

How it is asked

6 question styles you will meet

Name the style in the first five seconds. Each style has its own method.

One row

Draw boxes.
Circular

Fix one person.

Pair the opposites.

Read off the diagram.
Ordering

Treat it as a row.
The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Draw before you read twice

Sketch boxes or a circle immediately.

Why it worksA diagram holds the information so that your mind does not have to.

2Start with the most definite clue

An end seat or a fixed position beats a relative clue.

Why it worksA fixed placement removes options for everyone else.

3Use n + 1 for the position from the other end

5th from the left in a row of 20 is 16th from the right.

Why it worksThe left count plus the right count counts the person twice, so the total is n + 1.

4Resolve the facing direction first

Mark which way each person faces before using left or right.

Why it worksLeft and right depend on the person's own facing direction.

5Try both options when a clue allows two

If X sits on either side of Y, draw both and let later clues choose.

Why it worksA later clue removes one branch, so keeping both is safe.

6Circular: fix one person

Place one person at a fixed seat and arrange the others relative to that person.

Why it worksIn a circle the seats are identical until one person is fixed, which removes duplicate rotations.

7Treat 'sit together' as a block

'A and B sit together' can be treated as one unit.

Why it worksBlocks reduce the number of items to arrange.

8Count the seats between

Seats between two people = the difference of their positions − 1.

Why it worksPositions are numbered consecutively.

9Use symmetry in a circle

In a circle only relative positions matter, so fix one person.

Why it worksRotations of the same arrangement are identical.

One-line method
Identify the layout → draw it → place the most definite clue → add relative clues → check every clue.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Row
Five people sit in a row. C is at the leftmost end, B is two seats to the right of C and D sits immediately left of B
1C is in seat 1, so B is in seat 3.
2D sits immediately left of B, so D is in seat 2.
Order so far: C, D, B in seats 1, 2, 3.
Example 2 · Position from the other end
A person is 5th from the left in a row of 20. Find the position from the right
1Left position + right position = n + 1 = 21.
221 − 5.
Position from the right = 16th.
Example 3 · People between
Find how many people sit between the people in seats 3 and 9
1People between = |9 − 3| − 1.
2Seats 4 to 8 lie between them.
5 people.
Example 4 · Circle
Eight people sit around a circle facing the centre. Find the seat opposite to seat 2
1In a circle of 8, opposite means 4 seats away.
22 + 4 = 6.
The opposite seat is seat 6.
Example 5 · Arrangements
Find the number of ways 5 people can sit around a circular table
1Fix one person to remove rotations.
2Arrange the other 4 people in 4! ways.
Ways = 24.
Example 6 · Counting between
In a row of 40 people, A is 12th from the left and B is 9th from the right. Find the number of people between A and B
1B from the left = 40 + 1 − 9 = 32.
2People between = 32 − 12 − 1.
19 people sit between A and B.
lr-06:
Syllogisms & Statement-Conclusion

Syllogisms test formal logic using quantifiers (All, Some, No) — the trap is trusting real-world plausibility instead of what's STRICTLY implied by the given statements. Venn diagrams are the fastest tool to avoid this trap.

Start here

What Syllogisms and Statement-Conclusion are about

A syllogism gives you two or more statements and asks which conclusions FOLLOW from them. The only thing that matters is what the statements strictly imply, never what is true in real life.

Four statement types, a few conversion rules and Venn diagrams are enough to solve every question.

4statement types
4conversion rules
5standard chains
45 starget per question
At a glance

Topic map: the key ideas in one picture

The flow

The method, step by step

Follow the same order every time. Each step feeds the next, so you never have to hold the whole problem in your head.

1
Standard form

Write each statement in standard form: All, No, Some, or Some-not.

2
Draw Venn diagrams

Draw a Venn diagram for each statement (more than one diagram if the statement allows).

3
Keep what always holds

Combine the diagrams and keep only the relations that hold in EVERY possible diagram.

4
Test the conclusions

Test each conclusion: it follows only if it is true in all the diagrams.

5
Either–Or check

If two conclusions are complementary and neither follows alone, check for 'Either–Or'.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Logic, not real life

A syllogism is judged by its form, not by the world. 'All dogs are cats' may be false in life but still be a valid premise. Reason only from the given statements and treat them as true.

The role of the middle term

In 'All A are B' and 'All B are C', the term B appears in both statements but not in the conclusion; it links them. A valid conclusion connects the other two terms, A and C. If the middle term is not shared properly, no certain conclusion exists.

Definite and possible conclusions

A conclusion follows only if it is true in every diagram. A 'possibility' conclusion holds if it is true in at least one diagram. Many exam options hinge on that difference, so test each conclusion against both.

How it is asked

6 question styles you will meet

Name the style in the first five seconds. Each style has its own method.

Two statements, two conclusions
All roses are flowers; all flowers are plants; test the conclusions
Draw the Venn diagram.
Possibility
A conclusion that 'can be true'
True in at least one diagram.
Either–Or
Two complementary conclusions
Neither follows alone.
Three statements
A longer chain of statements
Combine two at a time.
Reverse trap
A conclusion that reverses an 'All' statement
Reject it.
With 'No'

Separate circles.
The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Draw a Venn diagram for every statement

All = inside, No = separate circles, Some = overlap.

Why it worksA picture shows what must be true and what is only possible.

2'All A are B' does not mean 'All B are A'

'All cats are animals' does not mean 'All animals are cats'.

Why it worksA can sit inside B with room to spare, so B has members outside A.

3Only 'Some' and 'No' convert exactly

Some A are B gives Some B are A. No A is B gives No B is A.

Why it worksOverlap and separation are symmetric relations.

4A conclusion follows only if it holds in ALL diagrams

If it is true in one diagram but false in another, it does not follow.

Why it worksThe statements allow every diagram that fits them, so 'follows' means true in each.

5Ignore real-world knowledge

'Some doctors are lions' may be false in life but valid if the statements say so.

Why it worksThe exam tests logic, not facts.

6Either–Or: complementary pairs

'Some A are B' and 'No A is B' together cover every case.

Why it worksOne of them must be true, so if neither follows alone, 'either or' follows.

7Some plus All gives Some

Some A are B and All B are C give Some A are C.

Why it worksThe overlap sits inside B, which sits inside C.

8No plus All gives Some-not

No A is B and All B are C give Some C are not A.

Why it worksThe B members inside C are not A.

9Two negatives give nothing

No A is B and No B is C: there is no definite conclusion.

Why it worksBoth being separate says nothing about A and C.

One-line method
Standard form → Venn diagram → keep what holds in every diagram → test each conclusion.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · Chain
All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Find the conclusion
1The middle term 'flowers' links the statements: roses sit inside flowers.
2Flowers sit inside plants, so roses sit inside plants.
Conclusion: All roses are plants.
Example 2 · Some and All
Some A are B. All B are C. Find the A–C relation
1'Some A are B' guarantees an overlap between A and B.
2All of B is inside C, so that overlap is inside C.
Conclusion: Some A are C.
Example 3 · With No
All dogs are animals. No animal is a stone. Test the conclusion No dog is a stone
1Dogs sit inside animals.
2Animals and stones are separate, so dogs and stones are separate.
No dog is a stone follows.
Example 4 · Reverse trap
Statement: All cats are animals. Test the conclusion All animals are cats
1Draw the cats circle inside the animals circle.
2Animals may include dogs and horses outside the cats circle.
The conclusion does not follow.
Example 5 · Conversion
Statement: Some pens are books. Test Some books are pens and All pens are books
1'Some pens are books' converts exactly, so Some books are pens follows.
2'All pens are books' needs the pen circle fully inside books, which is not guaranteed.
Only 'Some books are pens' follows.
Example 6 · Two negatives
Statements: No A is B and No B is C. Test the conclusion 'No A is C'
1Draw A and B separate, and B and C separate.
2A and C may overlap or stay separate.
The conclusion does not follow.
lr-07:
Venn Diagrams & Data Sufficiency

Venn diagrams turn abstract syllogism statements into pictures — draw EVERY possible diagram consistent with the given statements before deciding what 'definitely' follows. Data sufficiency tests whether you have ENOUGH information, not whether you can solve it.

Start here

What Venn Diagrams and Data Sufficiency are about

Venn diagrams use circles to show how groups overlap. They turn statements and counting problems into pictures, so relationships and numbers can be read off directly. Data sufficiency asks whether the information given is ENOUGH to answer a question, not what the answer is.

Questions come in three forms: which diagram represents a set of words, how many belong to a region, and data sufficiency.

3kinds of relation
2 and 3set formulas
5sufficiency outcomes
45 starget per question
At a glance

Topic map: the key ideas in one picture

The flow

The method, step by step

Follow the same order every time. Each step feeds the next, so you never have to hold the whole problem in your head.

1
Identify the sets

Identify the sets and what each circle stands for.

2
Decide the relation

Decide the relation between the sets: one inside another, overlapping, or separate.

3
Fill from the centre

For counting, fill the smallest region first, starting with the overlap of all sets.

4
Use the formulas

Use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) and its three-set form.

5
Test sufficiency

For sufficiency, test each statement alone, then both together.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Circles as sets

Each circle holds the members of one set. The overlap holds members of both sets, nested circles show subsets, and separate circles show no common members. Words such as 'all', 'some' and 'no' map directly onto these pictures.

Counting regions

With two sets there are four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. With three sets there are eight regions. Start from the region of all sets, fill the pairs, then the singles, so no member is counted twice.

Data sufficiency logic

Sufficiency asks whether the given statements fix the answer to one value. A statement that allows two values is not sufficient. Combining statements can fix the value even when neither works alone; and if both together still leave two values, the data is not sufficient.

How it is asked

6 question styles you will meet

Name the style in the first five seconds. Each style has its own method.

Which diagram
Which Venn diagram represents Doctors, Humans, Animals
Think about subsets.
Region counting
How many play only cricket
Subtract the overlap.
Union and neither

Use the union formula.

Fill from the centre out.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Name each circle clearly

Label every circle with its set before drawing overlaps.

Why it worksUnlabelled circles lead to counting the wrong region.

2Fill the centre first

Start with the overlap of all sets, then the pairs, then the singles.

Why it worksThe centre is counted inside every other region, so it must be known before the rest.

3The union formula

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Why it worksAdding A and B counts the overlap twice, so one copy is subtracted.

4Nested circles for 'All'

All doctors are humans: draw doctors inside humans.

Why it worksEvery member of the inner set is also a member of the outer set.

5Sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together

Check Statement 1 alone, then Statement 2 alone, then both.

Why it worksThe outcome depends on which combination gives one unique answer.

6Sufficient means unique

x² = 16 gives x = ±4, two values, so it is not sufficient alone.

Why it worksOne answer is needed, and two possible answers mean the data is not enough.

7Total from four regions

Total = only A + only B + both + neither.

Why it worksThese four regions cover every member exactly once.

8Percent Venn diagrams

Treat the total as 100 and fill the regions in percent.

Why it worksPercentages combine exactly like counts.

9Exactly one of two

Exactly one = n(A) + n(B) − 2 n(A ∩ B).

Why it worksThe overlap is removed from both sets.

One-line method
Label the sets → decide the relation → fill from the centre → use the union formula → for sufficiency test alone and together.
Solved examples

6 solved examples, from easy to tricky

The numbered circles in the question line match the red-pen steps below it.

Example 1 · At least one
In a class, 40 play cricket, 25 play football and 10 play both. Find how many play at least one
1n(A ∪ B) = 40 + 25 − 10.
2The 10 who play both were counted twice, so subtract them once.
55 students.
Example 2 · Neither
Of 70 students, 55 play at least one game. Find how many play neither
1Neither = Total − (at least one).
270 − 55.
15 students play neither.
Example 3 · Only one
In the same class 40 play cricket and 10 play both. Find how many play only cricket
1Only cricket = cricket − both.
240 − 10.
30 play only cricket.
Example 4 · Choose the diagram
Choose the diagram for Doctors, Humans and Animals
1Every doctor is a human.
2Every human is an animal, so the circles are nested.
Three nested circles: Doctors inside Humans inside Animals.
Example 5 · Data sufficiency
Find x. Statement 1: x² = 16. Statement 2: x > 0.
1Alone, x² = 16 gives x = ±4, so Statement 1 alone is not sufficient. Alone, x > 0 gives no value.
2Together, x = 4.
Both together are needed.
Example 6 · Exactly one
In a group 40 like tea, 30 like coffee and 10 like both. Find how many like exactly one drink
1Exactly one = 40 + 30 − 2 × 10.
2= 70 − 20.
50 like exactly one drink.
